'Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink His blood, ye have no life in you' Cyril takes with full sacramental seriousness: this is not metaphor but ontological condition. The eucharistic eating-and-drinking is the necessary means by which the life of the incarnate Word is communicated to the believer's body and soul. Against any spiritualizing reading that would dissolve the verse into mere faith-receptive metaphor, Cyril insists the verse means what it says: the actual flesh and blood of Christ, sacramentally present, must be actually received. 'Ye have no life in you' (ouk echete zōēn en heautois) is the privative consequence of refusing the eucharistic gift. This is the locus classicus of Cyril's eucharistic theology that the Tewahedo Anaphora preserves verbatim.

'Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day' Cyril reads as the eucharistic guarantee of bodily resurrection. The flesh of Christ communicated to the believer's body becomes the seed of the resurrection body — Cyril's standard formula is that the eucharist is the 'medicine of immortality' (pharmakon athanasias, from Ignatius). The 'I will raise him up' is Christ's personal promise tied to the eucharistic reception: the body that has received the Body of Christ has within it the seed of eschatological transformation. This verse anchors Cyril's distinctive contribution to eucharistic theology: the sacrament does not merely commemorate or symbolize, it actually communicates the resurrection life.

'For my flesh is meat indeed (alēthōs), and my blood is drink indeed' Cyril takes as decisive against any reading that would weaken eucharistic realism. The Greek 'alēthōs' means 'truly / really / actually' — Christ here explicitly disqualifies any metaphorical or symbolic interpretation of His preceding words. Against the gnostics of his own era and against any anticipatory spiritualizing readings, Cyril insists: TRULY flesh, REALLY blood — the eucharistic gift IS what it appears to be on the level of substance, even while remaining bread and wine to the senses. This is Cyril's clearest articulation of what later Western scholasticism would call the doctrine of real presence (without scholastic categories of substance/accidents).

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing' Cyril famously handles with great care against capernaitic misreadings that would take 'eating the flesh' as cannibalistic physical consumption. The 'flesh' that profiteth nothing is fleshly-mode-of-understanding, not the actual flesh of Christ (which gives life). The verse means: receiving the eucharist with merely carnal comprehension — as if Christ's body were divided physically among communicants like ordinary food — is profitless. Only Spirit-quickened reception receives the gift as it truly is. This is Cyril's careful pneumatological qualification of his strong eucharistic realism: the realism is true, but its appropriation is spiritual, not crudely physical.
